q: Which principle describes the weekly high-dose treatment option for severe vitamin D deficiency in Hazzard?
o: Continue high-dose replacement long term instead of changing to maintenance
Use a replacement course followed by a daily maintenance dose
Continue replacement until hypercalciuria appears, then change to maintenance
Start maintenance dosing and increase it when serum calcium rises
explanation:
Vitamin D replenishment restores depleted stores. Maintenance covers ongoing requirements after the deficit is corrected. **Use a limited weekly course, then switch to daily maintenance.**

**A. Indefinite high-dose therapy** — Continuing the loading dose after repletion adds risk of hypercalciuria and hypercalcemia.
**B. Replacement then maintenance** — One regimen is vitamin D2 50,000 IU weekly for eight to twelve weeks, followed by vitamin D3 800 to 1,000 IU daily.
**C. Wait for hypercalciuria** — Excess urinary calcium is an adverse effect and can predispose to stones.
**D. Increase when serum calcium rises** — Hypercalcemia warrants reassessment for excess dosing or another cause.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1540.
ref: Hazzard Ch 97 — AGING OF THE ENDOCRINE SYSTEM AND NON-THYROID ENDOCRINE DISORDERS

q: An 88-year-old woman with advanced COPD is seen in palliative care. She uses continuous oxygen and a wheelchair and needs assistance with all activities of daily living. Because of treatment burden, she asks to stop her medications, including prednisone taken daily for two years. What approach applies if chronic prednisone is discontinued?
o: Stop prednisone and monitor for recurrent respiratory symptoms
Stop prednisone and restart it if fatigue develops
Taper prednisone gradually to allow adrenal-axis recovery
Stop prednisone and reserve replacement for a future illness
explanation:
Daily prednisone can suppress endogenous ACTH and cortisol production for months. **If her goals and respiratory status allow withdrawal after two years, taper gradually and reassess as the dose approaches physiologic replacement.**

**A. Stop and watch breathing** — Monitoring COPD alone misses hypotension, weakness and gastrointestinal symptoms from cortisol deficiency.
**B. Stop and restart for fatigue** — Fatigue is nonspecific and an adrenal crisis may develop before a trial of oral prednisone is practical.
**C. Taper gradually** — A tailored taper reduces the risk of symptomatic deficiency while the adrenal axis recovers and allows respiratory symptoms to guide comfort care.
**D. Reserve steroids for future illness** — Basal cortisol can already be inadequate during withdrawal even before a new stressor occurs.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1531–1532. ESE/Endocrine Society glucocorticoid-induced adrenal insufficiency guideline (2024), recommendations 2.2–2.8.
ref: Hazzard Ch 97 — AGING OF THE ENDOCRINE SYSTEM AND NON-THYROID ENDOCRINE DISORDERS

q: A 76-year-old man has symptoms and repeatedly low testosterone levels supporting hypogonadism. Before treatment is started, which finding is explicitly listed as a contraindication to testosterone in Hazzard?
o: Reduced sexual desire developing over recent months.
Active prostate cancer under oncologic follow-up.
Low testosterone on repeated morning measurements.
Obesity with functional suppression of gonadotropins.
explanation:
Testosterone can stimulate androgen-sensitive prostate cancer. **Active prostate cancer precludes starting testosterone replacement in this man.**

**A. Reduced sexual desire** — This can prompt assessment for hypogonadism. It is nonspecific and carries no independent prohibition on treatment.
**B. Active prostate cancer** — Androgen exposure may stimulate the malignancy, including when the patient is already under oncologic follow-up.
**C. Repeatedly low morning testosterone** — This supplies the biochemical component of diagnosis in a symptomatic man.
**D. Obesity-related suppression** — Weight change and management of reversible contributors deserve attention. Obesity alone is not an absolute contraindication.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1533–1534, Tables 97-4 and 97-5.
ref: Hazzard Ch 97 — AGING OF THE ENDOCRINE SYSTEM AND NON-THYROID ENDOCRINE DISORDERS

q: An older woman receiving long-term corticosteroids for an inflammatory condition develops muscle weakness and wasting. Which pair of effects of glucocorticoid excess is described by Hazzard?
o: Muscle breakdown and increased bone resorption
Muscle building and increased bone resorption
Muscle breakdown and increased bone formation
Muscle building and increased bone formation
explanation:
Chronic glucocorticoid excess is catabolic. **It breaks down skeletal muscle and promotes bone loss, including increased resorption.**

**A. Muscle breakdown and increased resorption** — Muscle wasting explains the weakness. Loss of bone strength increases the risk of low-trauma fracture.
**B. Muscle building and increased resorption** — The bone effect fits, but excess glucocorticoids cause loss of proximal muscle.
**C. Muscle breakdown and increased formation** — The muscle effect fits, but glucocorticoids impair bone formation over time.
**D. Muscle building and increased formation** — Both tissues lose structural reserve with prolonged excess.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 769, 1530.
ref: Hazzard Ch 97 — AGING OF THE ENDOCRINE SYSTEM AND NON-THYROID ENDOCRINE DISORDERS

q: An 85-year-old man with fatigue and weakness is being evaluated for suspected adrenal insufficiency. Which distinction between primary and secondary adrenal insufficiency is described in Hazzard?
o: Secondary insufficiency typically causes mineralocorticoid deficiency because renin activity is suppressed.
Primary insufficiency typically causes both glucocorticoid deficiency and mineralocorticoid deficiency.
Primary insufficiency typically preserves aldosterone because the adrenal glands remain intact.
Secondary insufficiency typically preserves cortisol because the renin-angiotensin system remains active.
explanation:
Cortisol production depends on ACTH, whereas aldosterone is controlled mainly by the renin–angiotensin system and potassium. **Primary adrenal failure can therefore cause both cortisol and aldosterone deficiency.**

**A. Secondary failure and mineralocorticoid deficiency** — Loss of pituitary ACTH generally leaves the renin–angiotensin system intact.
**B. Primary failure and loss of both hormones** — Destruction of the adrenal cortex can impair both pathways. Salt loss and hyperkalemia favor a primary cause.
**C. Intact glands in primary failure** — Damage to the glands is the defining lesion in primary adrenal insufficiency.
**D. Preserved cortisol in secondary failure** — Cortisol falls when ACTH stimulation is inadequate, even if aldosterone remains sufficient.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1531–1532.
ref: Hazzard Ch 97 — AGING OF THE ENDOCRINE SYSTEM AND NON-THYROID ENDOCRINE DISORDERS

q: A patient with asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcemia receives conservative-management advice. Which approach accords with Hazzard?
o: Maintain hydration and avoid thiazides
Restrict fluid intake and avoid thiazides
Maintain adequate fluid intake and add a thiazide
Restrict fluid intake and add a thiazide
explanation:
Primary hyperparathyroidism raises calcium through autonomous PTH secretion. **Maintain euvolemia and avoid thiazides when possible in a patient with established hypercalcemia.**

**A. Hydrate and avoid thiazides** — Adequate fluid intake limits volume depletion. Thiazides reduce urinary calcium excretion and can exacerbate hypercalcemia.
**B. Restrict fluids and avoid thiazides** — Avoiding the drug is reasonable, but volume depletion can further increase calcium.
**C. Hydrate and add a thiazide** — Hydration helps, but adding a thiazide can counteract renal calcium clearance.
**D. Restrict fluids and add a thiazide** — Both measures can aggravate existing hypercalcemia.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1538.
ref: Hazzard Ch 97 — AGING OF THE ENDOCRINE SYSTEM AND NON-THYROID ENDOCRINE DISORDERS

q: A patient with cancer and diagnosed adrenal insufficiency is clinically stable and is not under acute physiologic stress. The patient receives regular hydrocortisone replacement. Which timing principle does Hazzard emphasize?
o: Schedule the doses in the afternoon and evening
Schedule the doses in the evening and at bedtime
Schedule the doses in the morning and at lunchtime
Schedule the doses at night and close to bedtime
explanation:
Normal cortisol secretion is highest near awakening and falls toward midnight. **When stable replacement is divided into two doses, give the larger dose on waking and the smaller dose at lunchtime.**

**A. Afternoon and evening** — This misses the morning peak and exposes the patient to a substantial late dose.
**B. Evening and bedtime** — Both doses are concentrated when endogenous secretion should be falling, increasing insomnia risk.
**C. Morning and lunchtime** — A typical regimen is 15 mg on waking and 5 mg at lunch, individualized to clinical response.
**D. Night and bedtime** — Closely spaced late doses leave inadequate daytime coverage and can disrupt sleep.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1531–1532, Table 97-3.

q: An older adult with a history of prolonged corticosteroid treatment is being evaluated for possible adrenal insufficiency. Which assessment does Hazzard describe as the basis for a definitive diagnosis?
o: Measure basal serum cortisol to assess unstimulated adrenal hormone secretion.
Measure serum cortisol following corticotropin to assess stimulated adrenal secretion.
Measure TSH and free thyroxine to assess thyroid hormone secretion.
Measure fasting blood glucose to assess the current glycemic state.
explanation:
Cosyntropin is a synthetic ACTH analogue used to test whether the adrenal cortex can increase cortisol production when stimulated. **Measure serum cortisol after corticotropin to assess adrenal reserve.**

**A. Basal cortisol** — Morning cortisol can guide assessment of adrenal recovery. A borderline basal result alone does not measure stimulated reserve. Morning cortisol is usually the first test of recovery during a steroid taper when testing is needed.
**B. Stimulated cortisol** — A subnormal peak at thirty or sixty minutes supports insufficiency. Use the cutoff validated for the cortisol assay.
**C. Thyroid testing** — TSH and free thyroxine assess a different endocrine axis.
**D. Fasting glucose** — Hypoglycemia can accompany cortisol deficiency, but a glucose level cannot measure adrenal reserve.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1531. Endocrine Society primary adrenal insufficiency guideline, recommendation 2.1. ESE/Endocrine Society glucocorticoid-induced adrenal insufficiency guideline (2024), recommendations 2.7–2.8.
ref: Hazzard Ch 97 — AGING OF THE ENDOCRINE SYSTEM AND NON-THYROID ENDOCRINE DISORDERS

q: בן 85, מתלונן על חולשה, איבוד תיאבון, כאבי בטן ובחילה. במדידות חוזרות של לחץ דם נמדדו ערכים על הגבול הנמוך (95/65). בבדיקות המעבדה: מדד ויחידות החולה ערכים תקינים Na mmol/L 134 135-146 K mmol/L 5.1 3.5-5.3 CREATININE mg/dL 0.9 0.7-1.3 BUN mg/dL 24 5-25 שעה לאחר הזרקת 250 מק"ג CORTICOTROPIN רמת קורטיזול 10 mg/dL ( תקין מעל 18). מה ההמלצות לגבי הטיפול התרופתי?
o: טיפול ב- HYDROCORTISONE 20 מ"ג בבוקר + 10 מ"ג בערב
טיפול משולב ב- HYDROCORTISONE ו-FLUDROCORTISONE
בזמן מחלת חום יש לקחת טיפול פי 3 מהמינון הקבוע
טיפול ב- PREDNISONE במינון 10 מ"ג
explanation:
An inadequate cortisol rise after corticotropin identifies impaired adrenal reserve. Interpret the values as micrograms per deciliter: a stimulated cortisol of 10 is below the traditional threshold of 18 (about 500 nmol/L). The printed mg/dL unit would be a thousandfold error. Use the laboratory’s assay-specific cutoff. **Teach this patient to triple his usual glucocorticoid replacement during a significant febrile illness under his individualized sick-day plan.**

**A. Hydrocortisone 20 mg morning and 10 mg evening** — Thirty milligrams exceeds the usual stable daily replacement in older adults. A late dose can impair sleep.
**B. Hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone for everyone** — Fludrocortisone is for aldosterone deficiency in primary disease. The stimulation test alone cannot locate the defect.
**C. Triple replacement with fever** — For fever of at least 38.6°C (101.5°F), triple the usual dose for three days and seek medical review if still unwell. Vomiting or hemodynamic compromise requires urgent parenteral coverage.
**D. Prednisone 10 mg daily** — This is excessive for routine physiologic replacement in most older patients.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1531–1532, Table 97-3. Endocrine Society primary adrenal insufficiency guideline, recommendation 2.1 and Table 3.

q: A 68-year-old man reports fatigue, reduced libido, and mild depression. One morning total testosterone measurement is 270 ng/dL. Which approach follows Hazzard's diagnostic requirements for late-onset hypogonadism?
o: Confirm hypogonadism from the single morning result and begin testosterone treatment
Repeat morning testosterone to establish a second low result alongside the symptoms
Confirm hypogonadism from reduced libido and fatigue without biochemical confirmation
Confirm hypogonadism from the single result because older age excludes other explanations
explanation:
Testosterone varies between mornings, and fatigue and low mood have many causes. **Repeat a preferably fasting morning testosterone before diagnosing hypogonadism from a single value of 270 ng/dL.**

**A. Diagnose and treat on one result** — A borderline individual result can reflect biological or assay variation.
**B. Repeat with symptoms in mind** — Persistent biochemical deficiency together with compatible symptoms supports diagnosis. Then assess cause and reversible contributors.
**C. Diagnose from symptoms alone** — Reduced libido is informative but neither it nor fatigue proves androgen deficiency.
**D. Assume age excludes alternatives** — Illness, medications, obesity, depression and sleep disturbance can coexist at this age.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1533–1534, Tables 97-4 and 97-5.

q: A 68-year-old man receives testosterone for diagnosed hypogonadism. Follow-up shows hematocrit above 54%, whereas it was normal before treatment. Which response follows Hazzard’s advice?
o: Reduce testosterone dosage and evaluate causes of hypoxia
Continue the same dosage and wait for the next annual blood count
Increase testosterone dosage and repeat the blood count at follow-up
Continue the same dosage and replace hematocrit monitoring with PSA
explanation:
Testosterone promotes red-cell production. A hematocrit above 54% during treatment requires action. **Reduce or interrupt testosterone and evaluate for hypoxia, including sleep apnea or chronic lung disease.**

**A. Reduce dose and investigate hypoxia** — This addresses drug exposure and another possible stimulus for erythrocytosis. Recheck the count before resuming or titrating.
**B. Wait for the annual count** — Annual surveillance applies when values are stable. A threshold has already been crossed.
**C. Increase the dose** — More androgen exposure can aggravate erythrocytosis.
**D. Replace counts with PSA** — PSA assesses prostate changes and cannot monitor red-cell mass.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1535–1536. Fifth International Consultation on Sexual Medicine (2024), testosterone monitoring.
ref: Hazzard Ch 97 — AGING OF THE ENDOCRINE SYSTEM AND NON-THYROID ENDOCRINE DISORDERS

q: A 68-year-old man receives testosterone for hypogonadism. During follow-up his hematocrit rises to 55%. Which treatment adjustment is consistent with Hazzard?
o: Maintain the current dose and resume annual hematocrit monitoring
Increase the current dose and reassess the response at follow-up
Reduce the dose or pause treatment until the hematocrit normalizes
Switch to a long-acting preparation while maintaining cumulative dosage
explanation:
Erythrocytosis is a dose-limiting effect of testosterone. **At hematocrit 55%, lower exposure or hold treatment, investigate contributing hypoxia and resume at a lower dose once the count is safe.**

**A. Maintain the annual schedule** — An elevated result needs timely intervention and repeat measurement.
**B. Increase the current dose** — This may raise hematocrit further.
**C. Reduce or pause treatment** — Interruption allows the count to fall. Reassess sleep apnea, lung disease and ongoing treatment benefit before restarting.
**D. Switch to long-acting testosterone** — Continued cumulative exposure does not correct the problem, and a long-acting preparation is harder to withdraw.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1535–1536.

q: A man with confirmed hypogonadism is considering testosterone treatment. Which cardiovascular history is specifically named by Hazzard as requiring caution before treatment?
o: Well-controlled hypertension without prior cardiovascular events
Myocardial infarction during the preceding six months
Stable asymptomatic coronary disease without a recent cardiac event
Well-treated dyslipidemia without clinical vascular disease
explanation:
Recent major cardiovascular events affect the timing of testosterone initiation. **Defer initiation after a myocardial infarction in the preceding six months.**

**A. Controlled hypertension** — Blood pressure should be followed, but stable control is different from a recent major cardiovascular event.
**B. Recent myocardial infarction** — A recent infarction or stroke falls within the six-month period singled out for avoiding initiation.
**C. Stable asymptomatic coronary disease** — Assess overall cardiovascular status and treatment goals. Stable disease does not itself meet the recent-event criterion.
**D. Treated dyslipidemia** — Dyslipidemia is a risk factor to manage, without the specific short-term implication of a recent infarction.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1534. Endocrine Society testosterone guideline, recommendation 2.2.
ref: Hazzard Ch 97 — AGING OF THE ENDOCRINE SYSTEM AND NON-THYROID ENDOCRINE DISORDERS

q: A 72-year-old man reports fatigue, reduced libido, and muscle weakness. His total testosterone is 310 ng/dL, reported as within the laboratory reference range, and his SHBG is elevated at 72 nmol/L. Which next step addresses the effect of altered SHBG on the evaluation for hypogonadism?
o: Obtain an accurate free testosterone measurement to clarify the biochemical assessment.
Start testosterone replacement on the basis of his symptoms before biochemical confirmation.
Measure LH and FSH in place of further assessment of testosterone concentrations.
Exclude hypogonadism on the basis of the reported normal total testosterone result.
explanation:
Sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) binds circulating testosterone. When SHBG is elevated, total testosterone can appear reassuring even though the free fraction is low. **Obtain free testosterone by equilibrium dialysis or a validated calculation.**

**A. Measure free testosterone** — This addresses the binding abnormality directly and helps interpret the borderline total value alongside symptoms and repeat morning testing.
**B. Start treatment from symptoms** — Fatigue, low libido and weakness also accompany other common disorders.
**C. Replace testosterone testing with gonadotropins** — LH and FSH help localize confirmed hypogonadism. They cannot quantify the free testosterone concentration.
**D. Exclude deficiency using total testosterone** — A total value within a laboratory interval may obscure low free testosterone when SHBG is high.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1533–1534.

q: Which combination is required to diagnose hypogonadism in an older man according to Hazzard?
o: Compatible symptoms and repeatedly low morning testosterone.
Compatible symptoms and repeatedly normal morning testosterone.
Absent symptoms and repeatedly low morning testosterone.
Absent symptoms and repeatedly normal morning testosterone.
explanation:
Clinical hypogonadism combines a compatible clinical syndrome with biochemical evidence of androgen deficiency. **Look for symptoms or signs and consistently low testosterone on separate morning measurements.**

**A. Symptoms and repeated low levels** — The clinical and biochemical findings reinforce one another. Evaluate medications and reversible illness before deciding on treatment.
**B. Symptoms and repeated normal levels** — Consider other causes and assess accurate free testosterone if altered binding is suspected.
**C. No symptoms and repeated low levels** — Repeatedly low levels without symptoms or signs warrant evaluation for an underlying cause; biochemical results alone do not diagnose the clinical syndrome.
**D. No symptoms and repeated normal levels** — Neither the clinical nor the biochemical component is present.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1533–1534.
ref: Hazzard Ch 97 — AGING OF THE ENDOCRINE SYSTEM AND NON-THYROID ENDOCRINE DISORDERS
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders

q: A 68-year-old man with reduced libido has a low testosterone result on an initial morning sample. What is needed before establishing hypogonadism according to Hazzard?
o: Repeat morning testosterone testing together with clinical evaluation.
Diagnose hypogonadism from the symptom and the single result.
Start treatment and use the response to establish the diagnosis.
Diagnose hypogonadism from his age and the single result.
explanation:
A first low testosterone result can reflect temporary illness or day-to-day variation. **Repeat the morning measurement and assess whether symptoms and signs are consistent with androgen deficiency.**

**A. Repeat testing and clinical evaluation** — Prefer a fasting morning sample using a reliable assay, then look for functional or structural causes if deficiency persists.
**B. Diagnose from low libido and one sample** — One low result cannot establish that the abnormality is persistent.
**C. Use treatment response to diagnose** — An empirical trial exposes the patient to harm and symptom change is diagnostically nonspecific.
**D. Use age plus one result** — Age-related hormonal changes do not establish a symptomatic disorder.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1533–1534.
ref: Hazzard Ch 97 — AGING OF THE ENDOCRINE SYSTEM AND NON-THYROID ENDOCRINE DISORDERS

q: A 72-year-old man has received testosterone for hypogonadism for six months. Routine testing shows hemoglobin 18.9 g/dL and hematocrit 56%. Which testosterone-associated adverse effect is identified by hematocrit monitoring?
o: Development of testosterone-associated erythrocytosis
Development of testosterone-associated gynecomastia
Development of testosterone-associated peripheral edema
Development of testosterone-associated sleep apnea
explanation:
Hematocrit measures the fraction of blood volume occupied by red cells. Testosterone can increase red-cell production. **Hemoglobin 18.9 g/dL and hematocrit 56% during therapy identify erythrocytosis.**

**A. Erythrocytosis** — The blood count directly detects this complication. Reassess the dose, consider interruption and evaluate hypoxia.
**B. Gynecomastia** — Breast enlargement is assessed clinically. Hematocrit does not detect it.
**C. Peripheral edema** — Fluid retention is recognized from examination and weight change.
**D. Sleep apnea** — Apnea may contribute to erythrocytosis and merits evaluation, but the blood count alone cannot diagnose it.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1534–1536, Tables 97-6 and 97-7.

q: What is the most common cause of Cushing syndrome in older patients?
o: Rapid withdrawal of chronic glucocorticoids
A benign pituitary macroadenoma causing hormone deficiency
Iatrogenic supraphysiologic corticosteroid dosing
Autoimmune adrenalitis
explanation:
Exogenous glucocorticoids can produce the same catabolic phenotype as endogenous cortisol excess. **Supraphysiologic corticosteroid treatment is the leading cause of Cushing syndrome in older patients.**

**A. Rapid withdrawal** — Withdrawal can expose cortisol deficiency after suppression of endogenous production.
**B. Nonfunctioning macroadenoma with deficiency** — Compression may reduce pituitary hormone production. Cortisol excess of pituitary origin requires inappropriate ACTH secretion.
**C. Iatrogenic excess** — Exposure to doses above physiologic needs can cause bruising, proximal weakness and osteoporosis within a relatively short period.
**D. Autoimmune adrenalitis** — Adrenal destruction produces primary insufficiency.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1530–1531.
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders

q: What is the most common cause of adrenal insufficiency in older patients?
o: Autoimmune adrenalitis
Tuberculosis affecting the adrenal glands
Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage
Rapid discontinuation of chronic glucocorticoid therapy
explanation:
Prolonged glucocorticoid exposure suppresses ACTH, limiting adrenal cortisol production when medication is withdrawn. **Abrupt discontinuation of chronic glucocorticoids is the common precipitant of adrenal insufficiency in older adults.**

**A. Autoimmune adrenalitis** — This is an important cause of primary failure but does not account for most older patients with cortisol deficiency overall.
**B. Adrenal tuberculosis** — Bilateral infection can destroy the cortex. Its frequency depends on the setting.
**C. Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage** — Consider after severe hypotension, particularly in an anticoagulated patient. It is much less common than medication-related suppression.
**D. Rapid steroid withdrawal** — The external supply disappears before endogenous production has recovered. Tapering and stress instructions address this risk.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1531–1532.
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders

q: An older patient has a newly identified pituitary macroincidentaloma at least 1 cm in size. Which evaluation follows Hazzard’s recommendation for a lesion of this size?
o: Assess symptoms of hormone excess and serum prolactin, leaving the other pituitary hormone axes unassessed.
Assess pituitary hormone deficiency for a solid lesion, but omit that assessment if the lesion is cystic.
Arrange serial sellar imaging for anatomical follow-up, deferring the initial pituitary hormone deficiency assessment.
Assess hormone excess and prolactin, adding a careful evaluation for pituitary hormone deficiencies.
explanation:
A pituitary macroincidentaloma measures at least one centimeter and may compress functioning pituitary tissue. **Assess both hormone excess and deficiencies at presentation, including in large cystic lesions.**

**A. Excess and prolactin alone** — These tests can detect a secretory lesion but would miss central cortisol, thyroid or gonadal deficiency.
**B. Investigate only solid lesions** — Large cystic lesions can also compromise pituitary function.
**C. Serial imaging alone** — MRI tracks anatomy over time and cannot determine whether cortisol or thyroid replacement is needed today.
**D. Assess excess, prolactin and deficient axes** — Pair target hormones with their pituitary signals, for example free T4 with TSH or testosterone with LH and FSH, and assess morning cortisol.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1528–1529.
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders

q: What CT finding on an adrenal incidentaloma excludes malignancy and pheochromocytoma?
o: Any radiodensity in an incidentally discovered mass
An adrenal mass larger than 4 cm
Low radiodensity, below 10 Hounsfield units
Higher radiodensity requiring biochemical evaluation
explanation:
On unenhanced adrenal CT, intracellular lipid lowers the attenuation of a typical benign adenoma. **A homogeneous mass below 10 Hounsfield units has the characteristic benign pattern.**

**A. Any radiodensity** — Attenuation and homogeneity are central to deciding whether the lesion is indeterminate.
**B. Size greater than four centimeters** — Large size alone cannot exclude malignancy. Heterogeneity and suspicious attenuation increase concern.
**C. Low attenuation below 10 HU** — The contemporary threshold includes 10 HU on noncontrast CT in a homogeneous lesion. Pheochromocytoma is exceptionally unlikely with this appearance.
**D. Higher radiodensity** — Higher attenuation lacks this reassurance and can warrant biochemical and imaging evaluation.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1532. ESE/ENSAT adrenal incidentaloma guideline (2023), recommendations 2.3 and 3.9.
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders

q: Why is hematocrit monitored during testosterone treatment in an older man?
o: To detect treatment-induced erythrocytosis and guide dose reduction or interruption
To confirm cognitive improvement and guide escalation when memory is unchanged
To establish long-term cardiovascular safety and guide continuation without reassessment
To select a formulation that can be continued despite an adverse effect
explanation:
Testosterone stimulates erythropoiesis and can increase hematocrit beyond the safe treatment range. **Monitor the blood count to identify erythrocytosis and adjust or interrupt therapy.**

**A. Detect erythrocytosis** — Measure at baseline, after three to six months, then yearly while stable. A value above 54% calls for action and assessment for hypoxia.
**B. Measure cognitive improvement** — Cognition requires clinical assessment. Hematocrit measures red-cell concentration.
**C. Establish cardiovascular safety** — A normal hematocrit addresses one adverse effect and cannot establish the overall cardiovascular risk.
**D. Choose a formulation despite toxicity** — Changing formulation does not remove the need to address a high count. Long-acting preparations are harder to withdraw.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1535–1536.
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders

q: Is PSA/DRE monitoring recommended for a 74-year-old man starting testosterone therapy?
o: Yes - age 70 or older is the usual indication for routine PSA/DRE screening during therapy
No - such screening is not recommended at age 70 or older
No - starting testosterone generally removes screening from consideration even before age 70
Yes - short life expectancy strengthens the routine screening indication
explanation:
Prostate cancer screening seeks occult disease in someone without symptoms. The likelihood of benefit depends on age and life expectancy. **Routine PSA and digital rectal examination screening are generally unnecessary in a 74-year-old receiving testosterone.**

**A. Start routine screening at seventy** — Reaching seventy is not a reason to begin routine population screening.
**B. Omit routine screening at seventy or older** — This applies to asymptomatic screening. A new suspicious symptom or examination finding warrants diagnostic evaluation.
**C. Exclude screening at every age on testosterone** — Younger eligible men can choose monitoring after discussing potential benefit and harm.
**D. Screen more with a short life expectancy** — A shorter life expectancy reduces the opportunity to benefit from detecting slow-growing tumors.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1536.
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders

q: An older outpatient has primary hyperparathyroidism caused by a single parathyroid adenoma. Which process explains this disorder?
o: Compensatory PTH secretion in response to low serum calcium
Autonomous PTH secretion from abnormal parathyroid tissue
Parathyroid hyperplasia after longstanding severe secondary hyperparathyroidism
Specimen acidosis during delayed processing of an ionized-calcium sample
explanation:
A parathyroid adenoma releases PTH despite calcium concentrations that should suppress it. **Autonomous PTH secretion is the mechanism of primary hyperparathyroidism.**

**A. Compensation for low calcium** — This is secondary hyperparathyroidism, as can occur with vitamin D deficiency.
**B. Autonomous secretion** — A single adenoma is the most common cause. PTH can be elevated or inappropriately within the laboratory range during hypercalcemia.
**C. Hyperplasia after prolonged secondary disease** — This describes tertiary hyperparathyroidism, commonly following advanced chronic kidney disease.
**D. Sample acidosis** — Incorrect handling can alter measured ionized calcium. It cannot create chronic autonomous PTH secretion.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1536–1538.

q: What serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level defines vitamin D sufficiency per the American Geriatrics Society (used for fall/fracture prevention in frail older adults)?
o: Less than 12 ng/mL
Greater than 20 ng/mL
12 to 20 ng/mL
Greater than 30 ng/mL
explanation:
Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D is the usual marker of vitamin D stores. Proposed sufficiency thresholds depend on the population and outcome. **For frail older adults at high fall or fracture risk, the historical target corresponds most closely to the option above 30 ng/mL.**

**A. Below 12 ng/mL** — This is the Institute of Medicine deficiency range, far below the stated target.
**B. Above 20 ng/mL** — This is the Institute of Medicine sufficiency threshold described for general population bone health.
**C. 12 to 20 ng/mL** — The Institute of Medicine describes this interval as insufficient.
**D. Above 30 ng/mL** — This is the closest option to the historical 30 ng/mL minimum goal. It is not a universal indication to screen healthy adults or titrate every patient to this concentration.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1539. AGS vitamin D consensus statement (2014), doi:10.1111/jgs.12631. Endocrine Society guideline communication (2024), doi:10.1210/clinem/dgae322.
Key note: Hazzard says above 30 ng/mL. The original AGS statement calls 30 ng/mL the minimum goal, so exactly 30 also meets it.

q: איזה מהבאים היא אינדיקציה לטיפול בכריתת בלוטת יותרת התריס (Parathyroidectomy) באנשים מבוגרים עם היפרפאראתירואידיזם ראשוני?
o: צפיפות עצם עם T- Score פחות ממינוס 1
Calcium Score גבוה ב- CT קורונרים
איסוף שתן לסידן מעל 400 מ"ג ל- 24 שעות
סימני Chvostek Sign ו- Trousseau Sign
keySource: IMA 2025-Jun Basic official answer key after appeals, Q122
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders
explanation:
Parathyroid surgery treats autonomous PTH secretion when hypercalcemia or organ involvement makes definitive treatment appropriate. **A 24-hour urinary calcium above 400 mg represents marked hypercalciuria and is a renal indication for surgery.**

**A. T-score below minus one** — This broad cutoff includes mild osteopenia. The relevant skeletal criteria include osteoporosis or vertebral fracture.
**B. High coronary calcium score** — Coronary artery calcification measures atherosclerotic burden and does not substitute for renal imaging or urinary calcium.
**C. Urinary calcium above 400 mg per day** — This exceeds the sex-specific thresholds of 250 mg/day in women and 300 mg/day in men.
**D. Chvostek and Trousseau signs** — These signs of neuromuscular irritability suggest hypocalcemia.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1539, Table 97-10. Fifth International Workshop on Primary Hyperparathyroidism (2022), surgical recommendations.

q: איזו מהתרופות הבאות יכולה לגרום לעליה ברמת PROLACTIN?
o: RISPERIDONE
LERCANIDIPINE
ALENDRONATE
CLINDAMYCIN
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders
keySource: IMA 2023-Jun Basic official answer key after appeals, Q118
explanation:
Hypothalamic dopamine normally restrains pituitary prolactin secretion. **Risperidone can raise prolactin by blocking dopamine D2 receptors.**

**A. Risperidone** — This antipsychotic blocks the inhibitory dopaminergic signal to lactotrophs.
**B. Lercanidipine** — This dihydropyridine does not share the recognized association of verapamil with hyperprolactinemia.
**C. Alendronate** — This bisphosphonate suppresses osteoclastic bone resorption and is not a typical prolactin-raising medication.
**D. Clindamycin** — This antibiotic does not block dopaminergic control of prolactin.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1527–1528, Tables 97-1 and 97-2.

q: איזה מהסימפטומים הבאים יכול להיות מוסבר בעקבות PRIMARY HYPERPARATHYROIDISM?
o: חולשת שרירים דיסטלית
ירידה קוגניטיבית
כאבים בחזה
שלשול
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders
keySource: IMA 2023-Jun Basic official answer key after appeals, Q119
explanation:
Primary hyperparathyroidism can present with subtle symptoms of chronic hypercalcemia in an older adult. **Cognitive impairment can develop or worsen, although other causes should still be assessed.**

**A. Distal weakness** — The characteristic weakness is proximal, often more noticeable in the legs.
**B. Cognitive decline** — Hypercalcemia can affect cognition and mood. A rapid, severe rise in calcium can instead depress consciousness.
**C. Chest pain** — This requires its own evaluation and is not a characteristic manifestation of primary hyperparathyroidism.
**D. Diarrhea** — Constipation, nausea, anorexia or abdominal discomfort are more typical gastrointestinal effects.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1537–1538.

q: איזה משפט מתאר נכון את תהליך בירור האטיולוגיה של היפרקלצמיה?
o: רמת 1,25 (OH)2D מוגברת שוללת ממאירות כגורם להיפרקלצמיה
PTH גבוה בנוכחות אי ספיקה כלייתית מתאים להיפרפרתירואידיזם שלישוני
Milk-alkali syndrome מתאפיין ב- PTH מוגבר
בהיפרקלצמיה משנית לטיפול בתיאזידים רמת PTH גבוהה
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders
keySource: IMA 2023-Jun Basic official answer key after appeals, Q136
explanation:
PTH should fall in hypercalcemia. Persistent PTH elevation suggests a PTH-dependent process. **Hypercalcemia with high PTH in longstanding advanced renal failure is compatible with tertiary hyperparathyroidism.**

**A. Elevated calcitriol excludes malignancy** — Lymphoma can raise calcitriol and cause PTH-independent hypercalcemia.
**B. High PTH with renal failure** — Prolonged secondary hyperparathyroidism can become autonomous and raise calcium. Renal insufficiency alone is insufficient to identify the mechanism.
**C. High PTH in milk-alkali syndrome** — Calcium and absorbable alkali cause PTH-independent hypercalcemia, which should suppress PTH.
**D. High PTH from a thiazide** — Thiazides reduce urinary calcium excretion. Persistent nonsuppressed PTH during hypercalcemia warrants investigation for coexisting parathyroid disease.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1536–1538, Table 97-9.
